# Git Merge vs Git Rebase

## What They Do

**Merge** joins two branches by creating a new "merge commit" that has two parents:
```
      A---B---C  feature
     /         \
D---E---F---G---H  main (after merge)
```

**Rebase** replays your commits on top of another branch, rewriting history:
```
              A'--B'--C'  feature (after rebase)
             /
D---E---F---G  main
```

---

## Core Difference

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserves exact history | Rewrites history |
| Commits | Adds a merge commit | Replays commits as new ones |
| SHA hashes | Unchanged | **Changed** (new commits) |
| Traceability | Shows when branches diverged | Linear, cleaner log |

---

## When to Use Each

### Use **Merge** when:
- Integrating a completed feature into `main`
- Working on a **shared/public branch** (never rebase these)
- You want to preserve the exact history of what happened and when
- Merging long-lived branches where context matters

```bash
git checkout main
git merge feature/my-feature
```

### Use **Rebase** when:
- Updating your **local feature branch** with latest changes from main
- Cleaning up messy local commits before a PR
- You want a linear, readable history
- Working on a **private branch** only you use

```bash
git checkout feature/my-feature
git rebase main
```

---

## The Golden Rule

> **Never rebase commits that exist outside your local repository**

If others have based work on your commits, rewriting those commits with rebase causes serious problems — their history diverges from yours and merging becomes painful.

---

## Practical Tradeoffs

### Merge pros/cons
```
✅ Safe — never rewrites history
✅ Preserves full context (when did branches diverge?)
✅ Simple to understand and undo
❌ Creates extra merge commits
❌ History can become tangled ("spaghetti history")
```

### Rebase pros/cons
```
✅ Clean, linear history — easier to read with git log
✅ Easier to use git bisect to find bugs
✅ No unnecessary merge commits
❌ Rewrites history — dangerous on shared branches
❌ Harder to recover from mistakes
❌ Loses context of when work was originally done
```

---

## Common Workflows

### Workflow 1: Rebase locally, merge to main
```bash
# Keep your feature branch current
git checkout feature/login
git rebase main          # clean up your local history

# When done, merge to main
git checkout main
git merge feature/login  # or use a PR
```

### Workflow 2: Interactive rebase to clean up commits
```bash
# Squash/edit your last 3 commits before sharing
git rebase -i HEAD~3
```
This lets you combine, reorder, or reword commits — very useful before opening a PR.

### Workflow 3: Merge only (simpler teams)
```bash
# Just always merge — safe and straightforward
git merge main           # update feature branch
git merge feature/login  # integrate when done
```

---

## Quick Decision Guide

```
Is the branch public/shared?
  YES → Always use merge
  NO  → Is history cleanliness important?
          YES → Rebase (then merge)
          NO  → Either works, merge is safer
```

---

## Bottom Line

- **Merge** = safe, honest, preserves history — good default
- **Rebase** = clean, linear history — powerful but requires discipline
- Many teams use **both**: rebase locally to keep branches tidy, merge to integrate into main

The most important thing is agreeing on a consistent workflow with your team.
